entry.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker
entry.content:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.

Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.

The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.

Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”

Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.

This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.

Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.

His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”

Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.

The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.

The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entry.title: Fossil CO2 emissions decrease in 2026
entry.content:
Fossil CO2 emissions decrease in 2026

Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026 – driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict – according to new research by the Global Carbon Project.

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget projects 38.2 billion tonnes of fossil carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions this year.

Emissions from oil are projected to decrease by 1.9% – likely a short-term response to the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict.

While global energy demand continues to rise, two thirds of the increase is being met by increased solar and wind power and electric vehicles.

However, the report – published alongside a new paper in the journal Nature Climate Change – finds that clean energy growth is not yet fast enough for a durable decline in global fossil CO2 emissions.

With emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) projected to increase slightly this year, total CO2 emissions are projected to be 43.3 billion tonnes in 2026 – up from 42.8 billion tonnes last year.

The remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels) is now 150 billion tonnes – equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

With CO2 still rapidly accumulating in the atmosphere, the dangerous impacts of climate change continue to increase.

The report also assesses natural “sinks” (absorption of CO2 by land and ocean). It finds that the land sink returned to former levels after a severe weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño weather pattern.

However, the powerful 2026 El Niño is expected to have a significant impact in the coming year.

The research team included the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), Alfred-Wegener-Institut and more than 90 other institutions around the world.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study.

“The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”

Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at UEA’s School of Environmental Sciences – who led the new analysis published in Nature Climate Change – said: “Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years.”

Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions”.

Professor Julia Pongratz, at LMU’s Department of Geography, said: “Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now.”

Other key findings from the 2026 Global Carbon Budget include:

China’s emissions in 2026 are projected to decrease by 0.9%, following twoyears of low emissions growth. In addition to a strong decrease in oil emissions,coal emissions rose slightly (0.3%) and electricity generation from renewablescontinues to grow strongly. While China produces 32% of global fossil emissions, it is also the countrymost active in deploying clean technologies and increasing carbon sinksthrough reforestation. Half of the global emissions avoided due to renewableenergy and electric vehicles are in China, which also has the largest carbonuptake through reforestation and afforestation (new forests). The USA’s emissions are projected to decrease by 1.3%, mainly due to adecrease in coal emissions (which spiked last year due to high natural gas pricesand cold weather). India’s emissions are projected to increase by 4.4% – higher than the 3.5%average annual growth over the last decade. European Union emissions are projected to decrease by 1.5%. Japan’s emissions are projected to decrease by 1%. Emissions for the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%. Thelargest component of the decline is in oil, likely driven by increased prices andglobal supply constraints. Projected 2026 emissions for the different fossil fuels are: oil down 1.9%,natural gas down 0.3%, coal up 0.6%. Emissions from international aviation and international shipping are bothprojected to decrease by 1%. Aviation’s decline is partly due to reduced activityin the Middle East. Global CO2 emissions from land-use change have decreased in the past decadebut are projected to rise this year to 5.1 billion tonnes. This is driven by anincrease in emissions from peat fires (almost entirely ignited by humanactivities) and forest degradation in Southeast Asia, associated with drierconditions linked to the onset of El Niño conditions. Total CO2 emissions – the sum of fossil and land-use change emissions – havegrown more slowly in the past decade (0.3% per year), compared to the previousdecade (1.7% per year). Emissions from permanent deforestation remain high at around 3.8 billiontonnes of CO2 per year over 2016-25. Permanent removals throughreforestation and afforestation offset around half of the permanentdeforestation emissions. The largest carbon uptake through re/afforestation occurs in China, the EU27and the USA, with combined removals 0.8 billion tonnes CO2 per year.Substantial uptake through re/afforestation also occurs in other regions such asBrazil, Russia and Indonesia – but here it is outweighed by emissions fromdeforestation. Current levels of novel Carbon Dioxide Removal (excluding conventionalmeans such as reforestation) currently offset less than 30 minutes of annualfossil CO2 emissions. The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere is set to reach 427.7 ppm in 2026,54% above pre-industrial levels.

The analysis published in Nature Climate Change found:

With global energy demand growing, new emissions can be prevented (or“offset”) by simultaneous growth in clean energy. The paper makes a projectionfrom now to the end of 2028, finding that 64-79% of emissions from new demandwill be offset by new solar and wind power and electric vehicles. The number of countries reducing their emissions while growing their economiesis clearly increasing: 59 countries emitted less in 2025 than before the COVID-19pandemic in 2019, while their economies grew. Even in countries where total emissions increased over the 2019-25 period,growth in emissions has slowed in all regions including in China, India and otheremerging economies. The effect of electric vehicles is growing rapidly but remains small because thevehicle stock takes time to be replaced, with only about 10% of the car fleetelectrified in 2025 (or 6% excluding hybrids). Emissions avoided by solar and wind power rose from 0.28 billion tonnes in2010 to 4.1 billion tonnes in 2025, and a projected 4.6 billion tonnes in 2026. The authors conclude that: “If further acceleration of clean technologydeployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline inglobal CO2 emissions could be a few years away.”

The Global Carbon Budget report, produced by an international team of more than 140scientists, provides an annual, peer-reviewed update, building on establishedmethodologies in a fully transparent manner.

The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth SystemScience Data on November 10 as a pre-print, and later as a peer-reviewed paper.

The Nature Climate Change paper is entitled: “A further acceleration of clean energy isneeded for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline.”

entry.title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
entry.content:
AI usage generates a fragile codebase

I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it.

I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers.

Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame.

In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications.

By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop.

Four ways AI makes codebases fragile

Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase.

1. AI writes shallow tests

One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric.

2. AI writes overly complex ccode

AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand.

3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding

And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures.

4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar

AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code.

Four signs that you have a fragile codebase

If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase.

1. AI generated codebases have more incidents

When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers.

2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases

Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve.

3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users

When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing.

4. AI results in a poor user experience

And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification.

Products made for humans require a human touch

The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI.

entry.title: What constant surveillance is doing to children and parents
AlphaProof Code
entry.content:
Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth

How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signalâs cryptographic protocol â long considered to be a grand security challenge

Today, weâre sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages.

This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code, a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verificationâmathematically proving code runs correctly without flawsâis the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive.

Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.

How we verified Signal

AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it.

First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signalâs security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.

Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human â just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.

Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them.

But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties â such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised â down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex.

Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks â a task that historically takes expert teams years â proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified.

To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.

While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees.

The future of security

Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats.

Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software.

Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender, formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work.

We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below.

Acknowledgements

This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli.

We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and MartÃn Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. We also thank Tulsee Doshi, Four Flynn, Kate Olszewska, Alicia Huang, Andy Liu, Benoit Schillings, Raluca Ada Popa, Melvin Johnson, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Demis Hassabis, and Sundar Pichai for their support of the project.

entry.title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
entry.content:
Note

Access to this page requires authorization. You can try signing in or changing directories.

Access to this page requires authorization. You can try changing directories.

This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. It was last updated for release candidate 2 (RC 2).

Updated minimum hardware requirements

The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities.

Arm64 requirements

For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC, DOTPROD, LSE, RCPC, RCPC2, and RDMA instruction sets.

For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application.

For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10. Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC, which provides support for at least AdvSimd, CRC, LSE, RCPC, and RDMA, and covers the majority of hardware officially supported.

OS Previous JIT/AOT minimum New JIT/AOT minimum Previous R2R target New R2R target Apple Apple M1 (No change) Apple M1 (No change) Linux armv8.0-a (No change) armv8.0-a armv8.0-a + LSE Windows armv8.0-a armv8.0-a + LSE armv8.0-a armv8.2-a + RCPC
x86/x64 requirements

For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2. This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV, CX8, SSE, and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16, POPCNT, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, and SSE4.2. This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013.

The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX, AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged.

OS Previous JIT/AOT minimum New JIT/AOT minimum Previous R2R target New R2R target Apple x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 (No change) Linux x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v3 Windows x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v3
Impact

Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following:

The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets.

For ReadyToRun-capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device.

Reason for change

.NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance.

The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system.

For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated.

Runtime Async

.NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead.

Runtime Async is a preview feature. To opt in, add the following property to your project file:

<PropertyGroup> <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> </PropertyGroup>

A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async.

The .NET runtime libraries themselves are compiled with runtime-async=on. The runtime libraries no longer contain compiler-generated state machines and rely entirely on runtime-provided async. This makes it possible to migrate an entire app (with only library dependencies) to the new model, and it provides broad functional and performance validation of the feature. The product team welcomes any reportsâpositive or negativeâabout throughput and library size changes you observe.

.NET 11 also includes two additional improvements:

Covariant Task â Task<T> overrides: When a derived class returns Task<T> for a base method that returns Task, the runtime now generates a void-returning thunk that bridges the calling convention difference, so virtual dispatch works for both flavors. The same fix applies to NativeAOT. Inlining in crossgen2: Restrictions that prevented runtime-async methods from being inlined during ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation have been removed. All async tests pass with both crossgen2 and composite R2R, and inlining of await-less async calls (the synchronous fast path) is confirmed end-to-end.

Note

The DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync environment variables that previously controlled runtime-async behavior have been removed. To opt out of runtime-async per project, set <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> in your project file instead of relying on the environment variable.

Cleaner live stack traces

The most visible improvement is in live stack tracesâwhat profilers, debuggers, and new StackTrace() see during execution. With compiler-generated async, each async method produces multiple frames from state-machine infrastructure. With Runtime Async, the actual methods appear directly on the call stack.

// To enable runtime async, add the following to your .csproj: // <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> await OuterAsync(); static async Task OuterAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; await MiddleAsync(); } static async Task MiddleAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; await InnerAsync(); } static async Task InnerAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; Console.WriteLine(new StackTrace(fNeedFileInfo: true)); }

Without runtime-asyncâ13 frames, state-machine infrastructure visible:

at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) at Program.<Main>(String[] args)

With runtime-asyncâ5 frames, the real call chain:

at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24 at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14 at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8 at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3 at Program.<Main>(String[] args)

Note

Exception stack traces (from catch (Exception ex)) already look the same with or without Runtime Async, because existing ExceptionDispatchInfo cleanup in compiler-generated code handles that case. The improvement is in what you see during live execution.

This improvement benefits anything that inspects the live execution stack, including profiling tools, diagnostic logging, and the debugger call stack window.

NativeAOT and ReadyToRun support

Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and ReadyToRun compilation. This extends the feature beyond JIT-compiled code to ahead-of-time compiled scenarios. The runtime also reuses continuation objects more aggressively and avoids saving unchanged locals, reducing allocation pressure in async-heavy code.

Debugging improvements

Breakpoints now bind correctly inside runtime-async methods, and the debugger can step through await boundaries without jumping into compiler-generated infrastructure.

Runtime Async performance improvements

Runtime Async includes several performance improvements:

JIT async support: The JIT compiles a dedicated runtime-async version of a synchronous, task-returning method rather than delegating through a thunk. The JIT turns the method's tail calls into runtime-async calls and awaits the task that would otherwise be returned, eliminating an extra layer of indirection. Tail-merged suspension points: The JIT tail-merges async suspension points so generated code is smaller. Cached continuations: Continuations used for runtime-async callable task thunks are cached and reused. Pooled methods opt out: Methods that are already pooled opt out of runtime-async, avoiding redundant work. Tiered async compilation: Async versions now flow through tiered compilation, so hot async methods get tier 1 optimizations after warm-up. Task and ValueTask factory intrinsics: The JIT recognizes common factories, such as Task.FromResult, Task.CompletedTask, and ValueTask.FromResult, and folds them into faster async paths. Tail-await optimizations: Implicit tailcalls from async methods are enabled again when the method directly returns another async result, and await Task.Yield() avoids extra allocations in runtime-async paths. Async continuations without ExecutionContext

Async continuations can now opt out of ExecutionContext capture and restore. ExecutionContext carries ambient stateâsuch as AsyncLocal<T> valuesâacross await points. Every Task continuation previously captured a snapshot of the context and restored it before running, even when no AsyncLocal<T> state was in use and the restore was a no-op.

The runtime now detects when a continuation has nothing to restore and skips the capture/restore cycle entirely. Task, Task<T>, ValueTask, and ValueTask<T> all benefit from this change, as does the runtime-async implementation path. Applications that use ConfigureAwait(false) and AsyncLocal<T> sparingly see reduced overhead in high-throughput async code paths.

JIT improvements Bounds check elimination: The just-in-time (JIT) compiler now eliminates bounds checks for the common pattern where an index plus a constant is compared against a length, such as i + cns < len. It also eliminates more redundant bounds checks for index-from-end access (for example, values[^1]). These improvements reduce redundant checks in tight loops and improve throughput for array and span operations. Redundant checked context removal: The JIT can now prove and remove redundant checked arithmetic contextsâfor example, when a value is already known to be in range. This optimization eliminates unnecessary overflow checks in generated code. Switch expression folding: Multi-target switch expressions now fold into simpler branchless checks when the targets are a small set of constants, for example x is 0 or 1 or 2 or 3 or 4. Faster uint-to-float/double casts: Casting uint to float or double is faster on pre-AVX-512 x86 hardware. SVE2 intrinsics: New Arm SVE2 (Scalable Vector Extension 2) intrinsics are available: ShiftRightLogicalNarrowingSaturate(Even|Odd). These expand the set of vectorized operations available on Arm hardware that supports SVE2. Math.BigMul on x64: Math.BigMul(long, long, out long) is now significantly faster on x64. The JIT generates a single MUL r/m64 instruction when both operands are 64-bit values and the caller requests the high half of the result, eliminating the previous helper call. Single-IG prolog restriction removed: The JIT no longer requires the function prolog to fit in a single instruction group (IG). Complex prologues with many saved registers, large stack allocations, or runtime-async state setup no longer trigger fallback paths. SELECT(cond, cns, cns) folding: The JIT now folds conditional selects whose two branches both produce the same constant into just that constantâfor example, condition ? 42 : 42 becomes 42. This fold eliminates unnecessary comparisons that can appear after earlier optimizations unify branches. AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics: System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.AvxVnni.V512 exposes 512-bit forms of the AVX-VNNI multiply-add intrinsics on CPUs with AVX512-VNNI support. Saturating floating-point conversions: Unchecked float and double conversions to small integer types now saturate to type bounds instead of wrapping through intermediate truncation. ARM64 Vector<T> by reference for SVE: When the runtime is compiled with ARM SVE support, Vector<T> values are passed by reference rather than by value, aligning with the ARM calling convention for scalable types and enabling better code generation for SVE-intensive code.

For better performance and code quality, .NET 11 adds several more JIT optimizations:

Constant-folding SequenceEqual

The JIT can now fold a string.Equals or ReadOnlySpan<T>.SequenceEqual call whose operands are both compile-time constants, replacing the byte-by-byte comparison with the constant true or false result. This matters most after inlining, when a caller passes another literal to a helper that compares against a known string. When IsAdmin is inlined into a caller that passes "Guest", the JIT sees "Guest" == "Admin" and folds it to false:

static bool IsAdmin(string role) => role == "Admin";

The optimization applies to string literals, const string fields, and UTF-8 literals (for example, "PNG"u8).

Devirtualization improvements

The JIT can now devirtualize generic virtual methods, including non-shared generic virtual methods and shared generic virtual methods that don't require a runtime lookup. Default interface methods declared on generic interfaces can now be devirtualized as well.

In addition, the result of Activator.CreateInstance<T>() is now treated as having an exact type, allowing the JIT to devirtualize subsequent calls made on the returned object.

These improvements unlock further downstream optimizations such as inlining and constant folding, reducing runtime dispatch overhead and improving performance. For example:

IfaceGeneric<string> caller = new Caller<string>(); Iface obj = Activator.CreateInstance<Impl>(); caller.DefaultImpl(obj, "test"); // Can be optimized down to Console.WriteLine("test") interface Iface { void GenericMethod<T>(T value); } interface IfaceGeneric<T> { void DefaultImpl(Iface obj, T value) => obj.GenericMethod(value); } class Impl : Iface { public void GenericMethod<T>(T value) => Console.WriteLine(value); } class Caller<T> : IfaceGeneric<T> { }

Here the JIT can determine the exact implementation behind both interface calls, devirtualize them, inline through the call chain, and ultimately fold the code down to the equivalent of Console.WriteLine("test").

Eliminating bounds checks after an empty-span guard

The JIT now picks up the length != 0 assertion from an empty-span check and uses it to prove the bounds check on the first element succeeds:

if (!span.IsEmpty && span[0] == value) { // The bounds check on span[0] is now eliminated. } Redundant branch and test elimination

When an outer predicate is already implied by an inner branch, the JIT now removes the redundant outer check. Similarly, when code assigns a value in a conditional and then immediately tests it, the second test is eliminated:

if (x > 0) { if (x > 1) S(); // The outer x > 0 check is folded away. } int y = condition ? 1 : 2; if (y == 1) A(); else B(); // The y == 1 test is eliminated; // each branch of the ternary goes directly to A() or B().

These optimizations are most visible after inlining, where guards from different methods land in the same compiled body.

Hardware intrinsics and code generation

.NET 11 includes several new hardware intrinsics and code generation improvements:

Hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions: The JIT uses hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions when the processor supports them. On x64, arithmetic uses AVX10.1, while conversions between Half and float can use F16C (available on most AVX2-capable hardware). On Arm64, arithmetic uses the optional FP16 instruction set, while conversions between Half and float or double use baseline Arm64 instructions. The optimization requires no application changes and preserves the existing ABI representation of Half. Better cost modeling for x86/x64 SIMD: The JIT's floating-point execution and size costs previously reflected x87-era assumptions. Updated costs that reflect modern SSE/AVX hardware let the JIT make better decisions about hoisting and common subexpression elimination (CSE) around SIMD code. Faster DotProduct on AVX: Lowering for Vector128.Dot-style operations now emits a mul + permute + add sequence instead of vdpps/vdppd when AVX is available, which is consistently faster. Faster IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher on Arm64: Arm64 versions of Vector*.Count, IndexOf, and LastIndexOf no longer route through ExtractMostSignificantBits, yielding a 5â50% improvement in workloads that use these APIs in their core loop. Arm64 ToScalar for 64-bit integers: ToScalar on Vector*<long> and Vector*<ulong> now uses fmov instead of umov, which is shorter and faster on most cores. SVE CreateWhile API expansion: CreateWhile gains signed, double, and single variants alongside the existing unsigned ones, completing the predicate-generation surface for SVE loops. New SVE2 and Arm64 instruction-set detection: The runtime now reports SVE_AES, SVE_SHA3, SVE_SM4, SHA3, and SM4 as separate instruction sets, allowing Sve2*.IsSupported queries for those features on capable hardware. AVX10 detection fix: The CPUID-bit cache for AVX10 was being overwritten by a later query, which could cause AVX10 to be misreported on capable hardware. This is now fixed. ReadyToRun improvements

Comparer<T>.Default and EqualityComparer<T>.Default are now specialized in ReadyToRun (R2R) images. Previously, the default comparers used reflection that R2R couldn't see ahead of time, causing callers to fall back to the JIT. R2R now generates a specialized helper in the imageâmirroring the NativeAOT approachâand benchmarks show up to a 20Ã improvement for collections operations that rely on the default comparer.

VM improvements Cached interface dispatch on non-JIT platforms: On platforms that lack JIT support, such as iOS, interface dispatch was falling back to an expensive generic fixup path. Cached dispatch yields up to 200x improvements in interface-heavy code on these targets. Guid.NewGuid() on Linux: Guid.NewGuid() on Linux now uses the getrandom() syscall with batch caching instead of reading from /dev/urandom, yielding approximately 12% throughput improvement for GUID generation. WebAssembly improvements

Browser and WebAssembly support has several improvements:

WebCIL payload loading: The runtime can now load WebCIL payloads directly, improving compatibility with browser-based deployment scenarios. Better debugging symbols: Symbol and stack trace quality for WebAssembly debugging has improved, making it easier to diagnose issues in browser-hosted .NET apps. float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> marshaling: float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> are now marshaled more directly across JavaScript boundaries, reducing overhead for interop-heavy code.

.NET includes improvements to CoreCLR-on-WebAssembly:

WebCIL V1 is the default for CoreCLR WASM builds: The shared WebCIL header gains a TableBase field (28 â 32 bytes). Both Mono and CoreCLR readers accept V0 and V1. Crossgen2's WasmObjectWriter produces V1 directly, and CoreCLR-flavored WASM SDK builds default WasmWebcilVersion to V1. Native re-link works for CoreCLR WASM apps: A full Emscripten-based pipeline replaces the previous stub targets. Re-linking dotnet.native.wasm from the runtime pack and including custom native code via NativeFileReference now works. JavaScript minification in Release builds: Browser CoreCLR Release builds ship minified JavaScript. NativeAOT publish for WASM no longer drops package satellites: Satellite assemblies from NuGet packages are now passed to ILC and pruned from the publish output, fixing localization for AOT-published apps that depend on packages such as System.CommandLine.

CoreCLR on WebAssembly now runs the libraries test suite end to end.

Platform support for more than 1024 CPUs

The .NET runtime can now initialize on machines with more than 1024 logical processors. Previously, sched_getaffinity was called with the default cpu_set_t (capped at 1024), causing initialization to fail on high-core-count servers. The runtime now allocates the CPU set dynamically. The GC retains its 1024-heap limit, but the CPU count limit is removed.

In-process crash report logging

A new in-process crash reporting mechanism captures diagnostic information from within the crashing process before it terminates. Previously, crash diagnostics were collected by an out-of-process monitor. While the out-of-process approach is safe, it can miss information that's only available inside the dying process. The new in-process path logs the managed stack trace, module list, and key runtime state to a well-known path before the process exits.

This capability originated on mobile platforms and is now also available on Linux and macOS. When DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump isn't enabled, set DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1 or DOTNET_EnableCrashReportOnly=1 to select the in-process reporter. Existing createdump behavior remains in place when minidumps are enabled.

NativeAOT: faster interface dispatch

NativeAOT now uses a dispatch helper for interface method calls. Instead of a direct fat-pointer call sequence, the runtime routes interface dispatch through a shared helper that can be patched to the correct implementation after the call site warms up. This reduces the binary size of interface call sites and improves throughput on workloads with many interface method calls.

Generic virtual method dispatch also uses the shared dispatch-cell infrastructure, which improves both monomorphic and polymorphic call performance. In addition, Assembly.GetCallingAssembly() now works on NativeAOT when stack trace data is available.

SIMD lane construction and composition

System.Runtime.Intrinsics now includes lane construction and composition APIs for hardware vector types. The new APIs let you construct a vector from individually specified lanes and extract or reorder lanes between vectors. This enables precise, portable control over SIMD vector element placement without falling back to platform-specific intrinsics.

The new methods fall into a few families:

Patterned construction: CreateGeometricSequence, CreateAlternatingSequence, and CreateHarmonicSequence build a vector from a starting value and a rule. Interleave and de-interleave: Zip, ZipLower/ZipUpper, Unzip, UnzipEven/UnzipOdd. Rearrange: The Concat family (ConcatLowerLower, ConcatLowerUpper, ConcatUpperLower, ConcatUpperUpper) and Reverse. using System.Runtime.Intrinsics; // {1, 2, 4, 8} â each lane is the previous lane times two Vector128<int> powers = Vector128.CreateGeometricSequence(1, 2); // Interleave two vectors lane-by-lane (Vector128<int> lower, Vector128<int> upper) = Vector128.Zip(Vector128.Create(1), Vector128.Create(2));

These APIs are available on Vector128<T>, Vector256<T>, Vector512<T>, Vector64<T>, and Vector<T>. They're building blocks for image processing, audio digital signal processing (DSP), and other SIMD-intensive workloads that need fine-grained control over vector element layout.

File locking on iOS and tvOS

On iOS and tvOS, including simulators, CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default. A FileStream that acquired an advisory lock could cause the operating system to terminate an app when the app entered the background while it held the lock. As a result, FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced by those locks on iOS and tvOS, including between handles in the same process. Mac Catalyst and other platforms keep their existing defaults.

If your app relies on FileShare enforcement and you accept the risk of suspension-related termination, restore file locking by using either of the following settings:

Set the DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING environment variable to 0.

Set the System.IO.DisableFileLocking runtime configuration property to false. For example, in the runtimeconfig.json file:

{ "configProperties": { "System.IO.DisableFileLocking": false } } Reliability fixes

The runtime includes fixes for the following issues:

On Linux, the SDK no longer crashes on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 on Arm64, and the runtime correctly traverses cgroup v2 memory limits at the root of the hierarchy. Generic virtual method dispatch no longer hangs after repeated AssemblyLoadContext unloads. TryDequeue no longer spuriously reports an empty queue while a segment freezes during growth. TryPeek has the same reliability fix. On Windows, garbage collection works correctly on machines with multiple CPU groups. Runtime diagnostics

The async profiler now instruments both runtime-async methods and compiler-generated async state-machine methods, so tools receive one consistent event model regardless of async implementation style. The runtime also adds improved interpreter perf-map logging support, and fixes parsing of CORECLR_NOTIFICATION_PROFILERS lists that don't end with a semicolon.

entry.title: Ableton Live 13
entry.content:
Ableton Live 13 adds new audio and MIDI workflows, sound design tools and mixing effects. Highlights include:

A built-in Step Sequencer, ARA 2 support for compatible audio-editing plug-ins, Capture Automation, and Contextual Browsing for adding devices and swapping presets directly from the device chain.

Drum Synth, new Multiband and Mid-Side Racks, expanded Rack controls, and Envelope Clips for automating and modulating effects on return tracks.

Device Slots in the mixer, and new Core Library Drum Racks, instrument presets, Audio Effect Racks, samples, and MIDI clips.

Arrangement Sync for Ableton Link, support for exporting tempo automation and time signature changes, and more precise event timing in exported MIDI files.

Mixer improvements including Send sliders, a persistent Mixer Configuration menu for choosing which sections are visible, smoother mixer resizing, and an Unsolo button on the Main track, plus an updated Phaser-Flanger interface.

Live 13 Suite also includes Melodyne essential, Looplet, Clipper, Transient Shaper and the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube.

Push 3 gains Custom Layouts, a new Step Sequencer layout, a new Performance Mixer, and Device Mode upgrades. Custom Layouts combine Session View, note areas, XYZ and mixer controls on a single page. The Step Sequencer brings the step editing experience from Live to the hardware. Device Mode adds jog wheel navigation and up to 32 Rack Macros.

Push 2 supports the new Step Sequencer and most Device Mode improvements (except jog wheel navigation), but not Custom Layouts, Performance Mixer or Expressive Step Editing.

Live 13 is the next major version of Ableton Live, following Live 12. It adds audio and MIDI workflows including ARA 2 support, Step Sequencer and Capture Automation, plus instruments and effects, expanded Rack controls, updated Core Library content, and more. Everything you can do in Live 12 you can still do in Live 13.

Ableton Live 13 comes in three editions: Intro, Standard and Suite.

They share the same core workflow but differ in their features and included instruments, effects and sounds. Live Intro is limited to 16 tracks and Scenes. Standard allows unlimited tracks and Scenes, and adds many more built-in instruments, effects and sounds.

Suite includes everything in Standard plus Max for Live, the complete instrument and effect collection, and Live’s full Core Library.

Suite also comes with Melodyne essential for ARA 2 editing, plus the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube and Looplet as free downloads at release. Compare editions in detail.

If you already own Live 12 – pre-order Live 13 at 20% off.

If you don’t own Live 12 yet – buy or upgrade to Live 12 at 20% off during the announcement offer and get the corresponding Live 13 edition free when it’s released.

Log in to your User Account and visit the Ableton shop to see the upgrade options for your license. From now until the release of Live 13, you can buy or upgrade to Live 12 and get the corresponding Live 13 edition for free on release day.

You can extend your existing plan to cover the cost of upgrading to Live 13 Suite and start using it as soon as it’s released. Visit the Ableton shop to see your upgrade options.

Most ARA 2 plug-ins work with Live 13, including Melodyne. Live 13 Suite comes with Melodyne essential. A small number have known compatibility issues. See the full Release Notes for more information.

One ARA plug-in can be used at a time, across multiple clips and tracks.

entry.title: The death knell of digital search
entry.content:
Lately, I’ve been having trouble finding stuff in my Gmail inbox. The Search function has become overzealous, jumping to summarize my conversations using artificial intelligence and skipping the actual addresses I’m attempting to search. It’s not just e-mail accounts, though; search is in crisis everywhere. Google Maps guesses where I want to go at a given time of day instead of simply listing places I’ve just searched for. When I try to use Google Search, the A.I.-overview function sometimes occupies my entire browser window, generating its own, not always correct, answers rather than directing me to relevant websites. Full-on A.I. mode skips the old blue links entirely.

Search has gotten so annoying, in fact, that it has become a problem for Google’s very business model. Companies pay Google to splash ads into search results that are relevant to their businesses—advertising stoves, say, to someone searching for kitchen-renovation tips. More than half of Google’s revenue comes from those ads. But, if users aren’t clicking through to external sites, because they’re relying on A.I. to answer their queries, then the ads that Google hosts are suddenly much less valuable. In a recent earnings call, Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, admitted that the company has been seeing “lower monetization” on A.I. searches. After the call, the stock of Alphabet, Google’s parent company, fell by nearly a quarter, down five hundred billion dollars, the largest single-day drop in its history. Even Google may not be too big to fail, as pessimism mounts about the possibility of Search ever again working the way it used to.

Just as Google has faltered in Search, use of OpenAI’s ChatGPT has surged. OpenAI’s consumer-product lead, Adam Fry, recently told the tech journalist Alex Kantrowitz that ChatGPT is siphoning users away from the older company: over the past year and a half, it has grown to handle one-fifth the volume of “search-like queries” that Google does. This acceleration only makes sense: a growing number of people now rely on A.I. chatbots as their primary windows to the internet, and they’re less likely to click out of those apps to ask the kinds of simple questions that they might once have turned to Google to answer. It doesn’t help that bots have lately grown much better at browsing the internet in real time, using virtual browsers and plug-ins, rather than simply generating answers from preëxisting data. Google has its own suite of A.I. products, Gemini, but they’ve lagged in popularity behind Anthropic’s Claude and ChatGPT. The investment firm Menlo Ventures found that Gemini accounts for only nine per cent of A.I. spending for businesses in 2026, down from twenty-one per cent last year.

Can the internet as we know it survive without a reliable flood of search traffic? Chatbots treat websites as databases of information to draw from, but since they divert traffic from those sites they don’t provide much impetus for creators to keep posting new content. The end state we’re heading toward seems to be an internet both generated and traversed by bots—in which case, it will no longer matter how annoying it is for a mere human being to find information. Some websites are already moving defensively to keep out the trawling bots attempting to digest their content. Reddit, one of the internet’s major remaining repositories of human-generated knowledge and opinions, is moving toward “a primarily logged-in experience,” as its C.E.O., Steve Huffman, recently announced. In a third-quarter letter to shareholders, Huffman noted that Reddit’s search traffic “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week” during October. The letter explained, “Web search is evolving from a gateway to the web to becoming an AI-powered destination itself.” In a recent earnings call, Huffman said that “people still want Reddit” but that “Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to.” Requiring users to log in is the equivalent of pulling up the drawbridge to keep away the A.I. models roaming outside. But it also means that the casual human searcher will be less likely to see the full conversations happening on Reddit.

In 2019, before the A.I. boom, the entrepreneur Yancey Strickler presciently outlined a “dark-forest theory of the internet.” As the web experience got worse, Strickler argued—because of “the ads, the tracking, the trolling, the hype, and other predatory behaviors”—users would retreat to more private, hidden online spaces, or “dark forests,” in search of human interaction. We once used search to find those dark forests and find the humans on the internet who were doing whatever we were interested in. Now those old tricks of Boolean operators and half-remembered keywords don’t work, because we’re meant to trust a robot to do the navigating for us instead. I often feel that the internet isn’t built for us human users anymore.

One prominent tech-commentator account on X has described companies as locked in “a knife fight for the remaining and dwindling volume of human traffic on the internet.” Many seem to have bought into the narrative that the old-school open internet is done for, so they’re scrambling to lock users into their own, A.I.-automated walled gardens. (Not to be left behind, Reddit is introducing an algorithmic For You feed and A.I.-generated short-form videos based on its content.) Google recently inspired a public backlash when it announced that it would make A.I. functions optional, rather than permanently accessible, on its software suite for schools and students, but with a catch: if schools turned off the Gemini A.I. functions, they would lose access to Google Search, too. This policy amounts to a threat: use generative A.I. or use nothing. The largest tech companies are investing so much capital in A.I. infrastructure—chips, data centers, intensively trained models—that they must make the bet pay off, one way or another.

The upshot is that, more often than not, I find myself using A.I. to fight back against aggressive A.I. Instead of using the Gmail app on my phone, I’ve been texting my questions about my own inbox to an A.I. agent called Instinct, which I recently granted access to my account. (It’s a security risk, to be sure, but one I was willing to take to see if the product is any good for techno-normies.) In a matter of seconds, Instinct can dig up an event invitation or a note from someone whose name I can’t quite remember. Instead of Googling potential interview subjects, I have Claude scrape for their contact information. But I would really prefer if Search just worked the way it did in the first place. ♦

entry.title: The Hardest Tarball?
entry.content:
The hardest tarball?

Nov 7th, 2026

Here is a curiosity: an archive that can be constructed using a single GNU tar invocation, that is extracted in 8 distinct ways depending on what tool you use.

$ printf hello > file $ touch empty $ tar --format=pax --pax-option='delete=?time,size:=512' \ --transform='s,^\./file$,cafÃ©,' \ -cf hardest.tar file ./file empty

It creates an archive hardest.tar from three files file ./file empty in sequence, where file is repeated so that GNU tar stores the second one as a hard link, and empty is empty. Exploiting the unique path of the second entry, the hard link is renamed to cafÃ©. This triggers tar to create a pax header to store the file name as UTF-8. We add a size=512 record to the pax header, which overrides the default size=0 from the hard link. The value 512 is not a coincidence: it is exactly the size of a tar header.

Visually, this archive has the following structure, with two basic interpretations based on whether a hard link can have a size or not.

Now, POSIX says that data blocks for a hard link “may be included” in pax archives, but the implications of this are not entirely clear. So the 512 bytes after the hard link are its data, and not the header of empty as we archived it? How can a hard link have different contents from its previous counterpart file?

Extracting it

This archive gives by far the richest and most surprising results I've encountered so far when extracting it with well-known tar utilities and libraries. The results below were produced using the latest releases of all packages at the time of writing.

GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go and Perl

This group is reasonable in principle: they ignore the size on the hard link, and extract file, its hard link cafÃ©, and empty.

bsdtar

This is the system tar utility of macOS, which is closer to POSIX in spirit regarding the concept of size on hard links, and writes the 512 bytes into the hard link. The end result is that file now contains the tar header of empty.

7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, and Rust's tar & astral-tokio-tar

This group agrees with bsdtar that the 512 bytes are data of the hard link, but doesn't write them into the hard link. Instead, they skip forward over the data, and you are left with just file and cafÃ©, without empty.

Java's Commons Compress

This is where you begin to need more imagination. Because cafÃ© contains data, a separate file is created that contains the header of empty as data, while file keeps its original contents.

PHP's PharData

Makes cafÃ© a separate, empty file, and also extracts empty. Why not?

RubyGems

Does not extract cafÃ© at all, but to make up for it, it creates an empty directory PaxHeaders next to file and empty.

R

R has an entirely different approach: it extracts empty with 512 null bytes. It mistakenly applies the size to empty instead of the hard link, and those 512 bytes are from an end-of-archive marker.

Bonus: Haskell

Haskell's tar would be exactly like GNU tar, if only it did not have string decoding issues, which turn the file cafÃ© into cafÃÂ© on disk (in the year 2026, this is not a rendering quirk of your browser).

.NET, Julia and uv's tar-codec

These implementations reject the tarball. I believe this is the best thing you can do, even if it's technically not POSIX-compliant.

More of this

This tarball is one of 134 tricky tarballs that I'm collecting and categorizing in my test suite haampie/tar-minefield, developed since the last post. Its website https://stoppels.ch/tar features a big table that shows how implementations deal with all these cases, as well as detailed info per test case. A variant from the tarball of this post is included as a test case.

If you'd like to discuss this, send me an email at firstname[at]lastname.ch.
