entry.title: Smart home devices should work without the internet
entry.content:
Smart home devices should work without the internet

4506 words23 min readSpencer Kittleson

AI;DR: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own.

TLDR; Nothing core in my house depends on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, the house keeps running. That’s been rule one for about ten years, and my other rules came out of it. This post has the rules, then both talks I’ve given on home automation, slide by slide.

Why local

My Nest integration worked until Google broke the API. That’s the failure I plan around now. The talks have a few more: a Samsung fridge showing a TLS certificate error on its own screen, and a Camp Chef grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show you the temperature.

Everything that matters runs on hardware I own. That’s Tasmota on ESP boards, an MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services, mostly Alexa and a few AWS ones. Alexa is just another way to flip a switch. If it’s down, the wall switches and the wall dashboard still work.

The rules

From the first talk, restated in the second:

No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Alexa can be a way in, but never the only way. Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. If someone tapes a wall switch on so a smart bulb keeps power, I skipped this rule. Be agile. Rooms get used differently and people move in and out, so it all has to be cheap to change. Check your automations. I once had four scheduled triggers hitting the same garden pump. Exceptions must be exceptional. I can break a rule, but only for a reason I’d still agree with six months later.

Added after year five, once more people lived in the house:

A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house. Config lives in one place instead of five vendor apps. More than one way in: an app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag. If I keep doing the same steps, they become a routine. Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point. No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. Nobody wants to swap a door sensor battery at 2am.

The build I get asked about most is the Tasmota sprinkler controller. It’s in both talks, and so is the garage door setup, which has been running about as long.

Talk One: Home Automation

Nobody needs any of this. I do it because I like building things that work in the background, and every automation is a small puzzle with a real payoff when it’s solved.

This is the backdrop for the whole talk. Phones, laptops, tablets, thermostats, and locks all talk to clouds that may or may not be up when you need them. Connectivity is fine. Just know what you’re opting into before you plug it in.

Most people start here with a thermostat, a plug, and a lock, and that’s a fine place to start. Each one ships with its own app and its own account.

Every device you add lands somewhere on this triangle. A cloud camera is cheap and convenient, and you pay for it with privacy. A switch I flash myself takes more setup time, and in return I can integrate it with anything. I figure out where a device lands before it goes in the cart.

Someone (often me) automates a light and then has to tape the wall switch on so the smart bulb always has power. If you’ve ever walked into a room and the switch did nothing, this is why.

The better fix for the taped switch is an in-wall Wi-Fi switch like this one. The wall switch keeps working the normal way and I still get a hook to automate. It takes more work to install than a smart plug, but nobody has to retrain their hand.

Rule one, and the one I don’t bend on. If the internet goes down, my lights still turn on.

Home automation is never done. Rooms get used differently, people move in and out, and new devices show up. Whatever you build has to be cheap to change.

The garage cooling flow starts from a manual trigger and checks whether the door is closed. From there it opens the door, waits, flips the fan on, or sends a notification if cooling is already running. It’s a small flow and it has kept the garage from baking more than once.

The door sensor and reed switch both report into a transform step that sets a global garage-closed flag and logs to Grafana. Below that is the chart from a few real days: 21 opens, with spikes showing when each one happened. Most people skip this part, and it’s the part that tells me whether I left the garage open without opening an app.

Four scheduled triggers all point at the same pump node. It’s easy to end up with five automations fighting over one device. Every so often I look at the flow and ask whether they still make sense together.

I’ve broken every one of these rules plenty of times. They’re guidelines.

Here are three ways to say “event in, action out.” Node-RED is my main tool. Alexa routines and IFTTT-style community applets cover the cases where I don’t want to build something from scratch.

MQTT is what keeps the pieces decoupled. The temperature sensor publishes and doesn’t care who’s listening. A phone and a backend system can both subscribe to the same topic, and the sensor needs no extra logic. The sprinkler controller in the Tasmota post is built on the same pattern.

The Sonoff Mini is small enough to hide inside the fireplace’s existing wiring. The flow lets either the dashboard or Alexa flip it. It makes the “memorable automations” list later because a fake fire you can turn on by voice makes a good party trick.

The whole sprinkler build fits on one slide: the relay and ESP module in the enclosure, the 3D board render, the Tasmota UI with BME280 sensor readings, the Node-RED schedule feeding the pump, and the finished PCB layout. The sprinkler post has the full writeup, including why I picked Tasmota over custom firmware.

The recap slide is the whole talk in five lines. I break the first one (don’t introduce a new way while removing the old way) carelessly more often than the others, and I regret it every time. The last one keeps the other four honest. “I was in a hurry” doesn’t count as exceptional.

The highlight reel: lights that blink when my heart rate is too low, sprinklers that skip watering if rain is coming, a garage that opens when my phone shows up but the car doesn’t, light and water for an indoor garden, an air quality sensor that kicks on a fan, backyard landscaping lighting, living room LED strips that shift between warm and cool, washer and dryer notifications based on power usage instead of a vendor app, 3D printer status lights, AC and heating monitoring, and a pile of AWS services (Alexa, Polly, S3, IoT, Cognito) stitched together along the way. The Nest integration gets a eulogy: “until Google broke the API.” Every home automation person writes that sentence eventually.

That was talk one. Almost everything on the “memorable automations” slide later picked up a new failure mode or got replaced, which is why there’s a sequel.

Talk Two: Home Automation, The Sequel

Enough time passed between the two talks that I had a different list of problems to talk about.

More devices means more decisions made without me in the loop. That’s a little unsettling, though mostly harmless.

First, a quick pass back through what talk one covered.

Same slide as before, with more icons on it now.

Everyone else is living this too. A fridge’s smart display throws a TLS certificate error. A grill controller needs Wi-Fi to tell you the temperature. Someone taped a note to a pole about an internet-connected printer they forgot to log out of. These are real devices.

These are the must and should rules from talk one with slightly tighter wording. I restated them because part of the audience hadn’t seen the first talk.

The rules stayed the same. The conditions they had to survive got harder.

A lot of my original setup assumed one person lived in the house. When that stopped being true, I had to patch a single-user system into a multi-user one, and the next few slides are what that looked like.

More people means more foot traffic and more physical keys to manage. Longer trips away raised the stakes on anything that could fail without anyone noticing. A water flooding scare is what finally got me to take leak and presence detection seriously.

Same joke with a new rule set. The first rules came after year one. These came after year five.

These are rules 6 through 11 at the top of this post. I wrote them after the house went from one person to several.

Next up are the concrete builds, which is my favorite part of any talk.

A motor-and-PVC-pipe rig for outdoor lighting, a UV grow light clipped onto a houseplant, and a UV strip under the cabinets for passive sanitizing. Each one solves a small, specific problem, and that’s where home automation earns its keep.

Same sprinkler slide as talk one. It’s back because it’s one of the few builds that never needed a rewrite.

A sensor that sits on a credenza, a robot vacuum that does the floors without anyone asking, and an AirGradient kit I assembled from a CO2 sensor, a particulate sensor, and a microcontroller, with its own small dashboard. The air quality kit has given me the most peace of mind of anything here.

This dashboard has replaced more apps in the house than anything else. It has a garage door toggle, a side door unlock, a front lock toggle, all lights on or off, brightness sliders, a coffee bar color picker, and a warm-to-cool slider for the living room. It all runs on one cheap tablet mounted next to the thermostat, so nobody has to dig through five apps.

The ambient lighting behind the TV is tied into the same automation system instead of having its own remote. It’s a small change with a big quality-of-life payoff.

Smart locks came out of the “more people, more keys” problem from a few slides back. The newer lock takes a password, the app, a keycard, or a mechanical key, so everyone in the house can use whatever they’re comfortable with.

The next few slides are the parts bin, for anyone who wants to build this themselves.

The ESP32 D1 mini handles anything custom. The smart plug is the off-the-shelf shortcut when I don’t need custom. The Pi 4 runs Node-RED and Grafana.

LED strips for ambient lighting, power transistors for higher-current loads, and small relay modules so a microcontroller can switch mains voltage safely.

The rest of the bin: a resistor assortment, color-coded wire so I can trace a circuit later, and a capacitor kit for smoothing and timing.

Node-RED handles flow logic and Grafana gives me visibility. Tasmota is the firmware on anything I flash myself, Telegram sends notifications, and Python or JavaScript fills in the glue code that doesn’t fit cleanly into a flow.

Here’s the garage flow today. The door sensor and reed switch feed a transform into Grafana and a global closed state. Toggle nodes publish straight to Tasmota command topics. Notifications fork to a Telegram sender and an audio chime, and a light-on counter resets at midnight. The editor tabs across the top (Lights, Sensors, Garage, Sprinkler, NFC Tags, Door Lock Security) show how much has grown since the single garage cooling flow in talk one.

I check this dashboard when I want to know if everything is okay. Humidity, temperature, dew point, pressure, and gas readings are on one side, and energy usage, door opens, and on-status history are on the other. I built it because I got tired of guessing.

Dashboards and Grafana panels work for me. Everyone else in the house just wants the light on.

Here’s the “multiple ways to interact” rule in hardware. The wall tablet is for whoever is standing near it. NFC tags and a QR code give a tap-to-trigger shortcut, and the Echo Dot is for anyone who would rather talk to the house.

Last section: the tools I use to build and debug all of the above.

A soldering iron for permanent connections, a 3D printer for enclosures and brackets you can’t buy, a multimeter for when something isn’t working, and a precision screwdriver kit for devices the manufacturer didn’t want opened.

That’s both talks, ten-plus years apart. The rules barely changed between them, while the list of problems they had to handle kept growing.

A third talk is coming, and this one is built around agentic use cases. The same rules still apply when an AI agent is the one flipping the switches, and I expect a few new ones once it is.

What readers told me

I shared the “no internet, no problem” rule on LinkedIn and asked for the most pointless internet dependency people had found in a device. Dozens of people answered. A Hacker News thread added more. Here’s what came back.

Everyone has one

Most examples were basic functions locked behind an app, an account, or a server:

A fridge whose temperature can’t be changed because of a bug in the manufacturer’s phone app. A TV that can’t even switch inputs when the internet is down, and another that has to be signed in before it works as a plain HDMI monitor. One reader’s older smart TV has dead apps but still works as a regular TV, which is how a device should fail. A heating system whose app doesn’t work from the local network. A kitchen vent and a dishwasher that need the internet even when you control them from Home Assistant. A smart plug that can’t be set up on an isolated network. Noise-cancelling headphones that search for a Bluetooth device forever, so you can’t just turn on the noise cancelling. Synthesizers and MIDI keyboards that need a cloud login for first use or firmware updates. A meat thermometer that only worked through its app and stopped working when the company went out of business.

The meat thermometer bothers me most. The hardware outlived the company, and it stopped working anyway.

Rules readers added Offline first, with the internet for extras. A device should do its main job on its own. Treat every third-party dependency as a risk. APIs change, so plan a local fallback or a clear degraded mode. One mobile developer works the same way: the core action works offline or from cache, and only the extras wait for a connection. Decide what must work offline. My answer is turning things on and off, temperature and safety controls, and anything a guest has to use without learning an app. As one reader said, if a visitor can’t turn something on or adjust the temperature without an app account, the design has failed. A stricter version of my first two rules: everything core works with the Wi-Fi or the automation server shut down, and smart features never take away the dumb ones. The wall switch should control the light directly and let automation flip it. A switch that only sends a request to the automation fails. That reader says my sprinkler controller fails this bar too. The only sprinkler controller they’d found with a local API and full control on the device itself was RainMachine, which is gone. Clean up when you throw things away. Remove a connected printer from your account first. An abandoned connected device can be an easy way in for an attacker. Practical tips Use local protocols. One reader recommends Zigbee and Z-Wave over Wi-Fi, because a switch that doesn’t need the cloud tends to behave the same year after year. Another uses Zigbee for the smart plugs that can’t be set up without internet. Let an LLM find the firmware. One reader buys the cheapest hardware that does the job, ignores reviews that complain about the app, and asks an LLM for local-first custom firmware once it arrives. That has worked for their switches, a thermostat, an air quality monitor, a thermometer, and a window fan. They’d have paid about 2.5x for hardware that was local out of the box. Old Nest thermostats have a way out. No Longer Evil is open source firmware for Nest Gen 1 and Gen 2 thermostats. Smart TVs can be tamed. Reset the TV and never connect it to the network, and the input problem goes away. Remote access is the cost of staying local. I use Tailscale on the router and keep the individual devices off the tailnet. One reader ran OpenVPN on OpenWrt, which worked but felt clunky, and is now trying Tailscale. There’s a gap to fill. One reader would happily pay for a pre-built, open “works with everything” Raspberry Pi image with MQTT. DietPi and OpenWrt come close and have a small footprint, but you need some understanding to get going. Another wanted a hub that ships with the house, like a water heater or a router. Home Assistant sells hub hardware that’s close to that. Right to repair is the bigger fight. Readers pointed to the right-to-repair movement and groups like the FULU Foundation, which work to keep companies from locking you out of what you bought. Counterpoints

Connectivity has real uses. A connected meat thermometer lets you watch the game while the steak cooks. The same reader also had an oven decide to update its software in the middle of cooking. One reader pointed out the business model behind all of this: companies would rather sell you a service than a product. Another expects the shift away from internet-connected devices to come from resilience worries rather than consumer complaints, since enough connected homes make a target. And one skips connected appliances entirely, keeping only computers and phones online.

Devices I’ve used

entry.title: Blender 5.3 released with Gaussian Splat support
entry.content:
Watch the Recap Video Make a Splat Gaussian Magic Point of View Radiant Future More About Shading CYCLES Divide and Shine CYCLES A diamondin the Rough CYCLES Gone with Denoise

NVIDIA DLSS brings near-final render quality to the viewport, making lighting and look development faster and more responsive while virtually eliminating flickering between frames during animation playback.

Find it in the Denoise panel under Render properties, Sampling.

DLSS denoising requires NVIDIA driver version 620 or newer.

EEVEE Lights Meet Material Nodes Lighting to Your Liking A Wider Perspective

EEVEE can now render panoramic cameras, supporting all types of projections, from equirectangular and cubemap formats to various fisheye models and mirror ball.

The current implementation has a few limitations: depth of field, raytracing, and volumetric temporal reprojection in the viewport are not yet supported.

More in EEVEE & Viewport COMPOSITOR Side Effects

You can now stack Effects on your scene just like you would modifiers or constraints.

Applying compositing effects has never been easier.

One-click, Bloom!

Choose from built-in effects such as Bloom, Chromatic Aberration, Film Grain, and Vignette, as well as effects from online asset libraries or your own custom compositor node groups.

Internally, each effect is its own node group, with its output passed on to the next effect.

You can further customize effects at any time in the Compositor editor.

COMPOSITOR Bundle Up

17 Geometry Nodes are now supported in the Compositor, bringing a range of new capabilities across bundles, math and logic, and utility operations.

This includes bundle support with Get Bundle Item, Store Bundle Item, Combine Bundle, Typed Bundle, and Separate Bundle.

Math and logic nodes such as Boolean Math, Compare, Float to Integer, Integer Math, Matrix SVD, Combine Transform, and Separate Transform. Plus utility nodes including Hash Value, Random Value, Is Viewport, Import Text, and Bone Info.

Play Fast

Playback is now up to 2x faster on GPU, particularly when playing back EXR sequences.

The interactive compositor now supports playback caching. It can be enabled from the sidebar, Options panel.

Anisotropic Kuwahara is now up to 10x faster on Apple GPUs, 2x faster on NVIDIA GPUs, and 25-30% on CPU.

More in Compositor Study the artwork

Blender splash artwork source files are available for you to play with!

CORE Blender, meet projects.

Until now, Blender’s preferences (such as asset libraries) were shared across all projects, and it was up to users to keep related files and resources organized.

Blender now supports projects, giving you a way to group related files, share resources, and manage settings across an entire project, whether you’re working alone or as part of a team.

EverythingEverywhereAll In a Project

Projects support custom variables that can be used throughout a project, such as a character’s name or a frequently used file path.

Per-project asset libraries and color management configurations are also supported. You can even set up a custom splash screen for your project, providing quick access to its files and other recent projects.

Add-ons and other extensions per-project will follow in future Blender versions.

Projects are entirely optional, most of the time you’ll probably work without one.

ASSETS Asset Libraries ♥ Extensions

Asset libraries can now be shared as extensions! Just like add-ons or themes.

Browse hundreds of public domain assets available on the Extensions platform via the Get Extensions tab and install them directly from within Blender.

GREASE PENCIL Drawn to Select

Draw Mode now has its own selection tools: Tweak, Lasso, Box, and Circle. Select strokes and adjust them right where you draw.

Move, rotate, scale, duplicate, copy, paste, and delete strokes using the usual shortcuts, or access all these actions from the new Stroke menu.

Carve Diem

Meet the new Carver tool in Draw Mode.

It cuts shapes using proper Boolean subtraction, creating clean cuts in strokes and fills based on a lasso selection. Holes are created automatically when needed.

When a shape has both a stroke and a fill, carving a hole into it also creates a stroke around the hole. Fills that are split apart become separate shapes, making them easy to sculpt further.

One Tool to Fill Them All

The Fill tool can now fill multiple regions at once.

Simply draw a path across multiple regions to fill them all as a single shape, with no gaps or borders in between.

Ramp It Up

Gradient fills now use a ColorRamp input instead of being limited to just two colors.

Flip Out

Mirror the camera view horizontally with the new Flip View operator to evaluate the composition from a different perspective and spot asymmetry or visual imbalances.

This only affects the viewport display. It does not change the camera object’s transform or the final render, which remains unchanged. Use the operator again to restore the original orientation.

Flip View has no shortcut assigned by default, but you can assign your own through the right-click menu or add it to Quick Favorites (Q) for easy access.

I/O USD Collection Importer

Collections can now be associated to importers.

Similar to the Collection Exporters introduced in Blender 4.2 LTS, Collection Importers make it easy to re-import data with a single click, without having to navigate menus or adjust settings repeatedly.

Configure them through the Importers panel under Collection Properties. Settings are stored in .blend files, making them easy to share and preserving them across Blender sessions.

Only the USD importer is supported in Blender 5.3.

See all USD, Alembic, glTF, OpenEXR, and other I/O changes.

VIDEO SEQUENCER Cut to the chase

The Video Sequencer gets a full ripple editing framework, a rewritten blade tool, and a long list of editing, interface, and performance improvements, including initial OpenTimelineIO support.

Ripple,Shuffle,Overwrite

Welcome Ripple editing to Blender 5.3!

This new overlap mode automatically moves strips forward or backward as edits are made, maintaining timeline continuity without the need to manually close gaps.

Ripple, Shuffle, and Overwrite modes are now consistently used across editing operations. Switch between them while moving strips using R, S, and V.

Making Waves

Complete the ripple workflow with these handy operators:

Ripple Add: Hold Shift while dragging and dropping strips to insert them using ripple behavior, automatically making room in the timeline.

Ripple Trim: Trim selected strips at the playhead and automatically close the resulting gaps. Use Shift+Q or Shift+W to trim from either side.

Ripple Delete: Delete selected strips and move subsequent content back to close the gaps. Use Shift+X.

Cutting Edge: Blade 2.0

Splits are now visualized as a line when using Blade and as a region when using Box Blade. Tooltips display frame values at the split location, while a real-time preview shows the frame beneath the cursor.

Press and hold C in the timeline to temporarily activate the Blade tool.Release it to switch back to the previously active tool.

But wait, there’s more: Hardware decoding, thumbnail support for Scene and other strips, OpenTimelineIO import and export, and much more.

USER INTERFACE Search. Sort. Scribble. Sorted Out

Arrange your objects freely with custom sorting in the Outliner. Finally.

Switch back to alphabetical order from the header popover.

Plus improvements to filtering, drag-and-drop behavior, and hierarchy management.

Side Quest

Sidebars in all editors now support search, making it possible to find any property or operator, even inside tabs created by add-ons.

Press Ctrl/Cmd + F while hovering the sidebar and start typing right away, or through the context menu of the tabs and panels.

To clear the search, press Alt/Option + F.

Mark it Down

The Blender UI now supports rendering basic Markdown formatting.

In node editors, write markdown directly in the new Comment node, or in regular layouts for scripts/add-ons through the label_markdown widget. Another handy widget for long strings is label_multiline, it behaves just like labels but allows text to wrap.

But wait: IME support, improved tooltips, box-select gesture, browsable node editor context paths, better Attribute Viewer overlay, Curve widget selection, and more!

What’s Next?

Blender on tablets, texture layers, animation layers? Show your support for upcoming development projects and help shape the future of Blender.

BUT WAIT, THERE’S MORE

Plus hundreds of bug fixes, code cleanups and refactors.See the full list of changes.

CREDITS

Blender is a community project.Learn more on how you can contribute to Blender.

List of developers who contributed to Blender 5.3 and all-time contributors.

Splash artwork: OVERGROWN, by Blender Studio

Cycles diamonds render by Chris Tyler. Butterflies specter shader by Cartesian Caramel. Grease Pencil drawings by Vivien Lulkowski from Blender Studio, Cowboi and Storm by Blender Studio.

Huge thanks to everyone involved! 🧡

entry.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
entry.content:
Hello you fine Internet folks,

Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture.

Hope y’all enjoy!

Overview

From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core.Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2.

At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4.

Branch Prediction

Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor.

The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5.

Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache.

When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB.

When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity.

The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor.

Instruction Fetch

Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters.

Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things.

Execution Engine

The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of.

On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs.

AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost.

On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well.

Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2.

The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split

In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed.

Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue.

The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330.

The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency.

Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB.

L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns.

Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle.

Load/Store

Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify.

A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.

SPEC CPU 2026 Performance

The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.

The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.

The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.

Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.

Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.

Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.

The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.

The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.

Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.

The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.

The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.

The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.

The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.

Final Words

The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.

However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.

The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.

AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

entry.title: Val Town is winding down
entry.content:
Dear Val Town community,

We’ve made the difficult decision to wind down Val Town.

You took a big leap of faith to build on us. We thank you for your trust, and we’re sorry we can’t continue to serve you.

The bad news about our business – that we couldn’t compete in the cloud computing space – is good news for you migrating off: there are many wonderful hosting providers you can migrate to, and today’s LLMs are great at these types of migrations. We have guides for migrating to Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, and Render. Please reach out if you need help at support@val.town or on Discord.

We are pausing billing today, and will continue servicing existing subscriptions for free. If you pre-paid for our annual plan, we will issue you a partial refund.

Here’s the timeline on our wind-down:

Service End of life date New signups and plan upgrades Nov 10, 2026 (today) Read-only mode (not including sqlite and blob storage) Dec 10, 2026 All other services Jan 10, 2027 Open-sourcing Val Town Feb 1, 2027

Thank you, the members of the Val Town team, for giving it your all over the past four years. Thank you Tom, Jackson, Charlie, Pete, Potluck, Charmaine, Max, Andre, Sophie, Wolf, Justin, Rodrigo and JP. It was an honor.

Thank you, Dan Levine, for being the best investor I could’ve asked for. Thank you, my other investors, for your trust, support, and capital.

Thank you, our customers and users, for building on us with passion and creativity.

Steve Krouse

entry.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
entry.content:
Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.

Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below.

# Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .

Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.

Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.

Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:

Modern Browser APIs: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.

We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).

View an example: the navigation-drawer guide.

We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is empirically proven and continuously calibrated so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline:

entry.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
entry.content:
Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN subscriber-only content] Welcome to LWN.net

The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN. Thank you for visiting LWN.net!

Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

Synaptics and Displaylink

The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.

The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.

A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.

Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.

Vino

He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome." He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve.

Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.

He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:

The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.

From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.

Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the "intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than "have the situation become more formal later". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK.

Cease and desist

On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not "substantially responded" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with "public statements and further development activities". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work.

Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of "any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent", withdrawing submissions of materials "made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization", and to identify in writing every location "in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.

Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "never lit a panel", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.

On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns."

He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to "reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software".

He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "interact with our respective OIN commitments", and expressed a desire to sort things out with Synaptics constructively. "I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities".

Lothian did not think he could "reasonably provide the signed undertaking" Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.

Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:

As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now we are escalating as we deem appropriate.

The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization.

Bateman sent a follow-up letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking "monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with.

Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "ideally with someone qualified to help me read them". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "DisplayLink is not a member of OIN" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.

OIN to the rescue?

Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.

OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components.

I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.

Status

Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. "Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics."

Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: "You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?'"

For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

entry.title: Work at the Frontier: AI's effect on freelance work
entry.content:
Work at the Frontier:AI’s effect on freelance work

New research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.

For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

The stakes are substantial. Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index(opens in a new window) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its previous annual study(opens in a new window) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

Freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

The mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

Many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

The remaining 20 work categories showed the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people currently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

By late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

Some clients asked for AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

Although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous Work at the Frontier papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Because freelance projects turn over quickly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a new job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

The findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.
